title: The Role of Enzyme Spatial Distribution in Enzyme Metal-Organic Frameworks using Cryogenic Electron Microscopy (CryoEM), Cryogenic Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (CryoEELS), and Energy-Filtered TEM (EF-TEM)
content: Enzymes provide a sustainable alternative to traditional catalysts in chemical synthesis and bioremediation [1]. However, their utility is often limited by their susceptibility to denaturation under non-native conditions, such as elevated temperatures, extreme pH levels, or exposure to organic solvents. Consequently, significant research has focused on developing materials that enhance enzyme stability. One promising approach is to replicate biomineralization—a natural process that forms hierarchically structured organic-inorganic composites with essential biological functions such as catalysis, storage, and protection [1]. Inspired by biomineralization, biomimetic crystallization has emerged as an effective strategy for developing hybrid materials such as enzyme-based metal-organic framework (E@MOF) biocomposites. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are crystalline, porous materials made of organic and inorganic components. Their exceptional versatility has made them highly valuable for applications in gas storage and separation, catalysis, chemical sensing, and drug delivery [1,2]. Enzyme encapsulation within MOFs is typically achieved by performing MOF synthesis in the presence of enzymes, which can mediate crystal nucleation and growth, facilitating their encapsulation. However, a critical knowledge gap remains in regards to how the precise spatial localization and distribution of encapsulated enzymes within MOF crystals influence their overall properties.
